title: Thomas Aquinas I: The Five Ways
subtitle: How a quiet friar married Aristotle to Christianity and tried to reason his way to God
objectives: By the end you will be able to explain how Aristotle's works returned to Latin Europe and why they caused both excitement and alarm.
By the end you will be able to describe Aquinas' view of how faith and reason relate, including the difference between preambles and articles of faith.
By the end you will be able to state each of the Five Ways in your own words and identify the pattern they share.
By the end you will be able to evaluate the strongest objections to the Five Ways and how defenders reply.
hook:
Imagine a university lecture hall in Paris in the 1250s. The students are young men in clerical robes, many of them training to be priests. The book causing all the excitement is not the Bible but the works of a pagan Greek who had died more than fifteen hundred years earlier: Aristotle. His logic, physics, biology, ethics and metaphysics had flooded into Europe in Latin translations, many made from Arabic, along with the commentaries of Avicenna and Averroes (Days 32–33). Some churchmen were thrilled. Others were alarmed: Aristotle taught that the world was eternal and seemed to doubt that individual souls survive death. Did Christians now have to choose between the Bible and the greatest scientist the world had known?

A large, quiet Dominican friar from southern Italy answered no. Thomas Aquinas spent his short life arguing that faith and reason, properly understood, could never truly conflict, and that reason, using Aristotle's tools, could prove that God exists. His most famous attempt fills barely two pages. It is known as the Five Ways.

sections.heading: The Dumb Ox
sections.body:
**Thomas Aquinas** was born around 1225 at the castle of Roccasecca, near the town of Aquino between Rome and Naples, into a noble family. At about five he was sent to the great Benedictine abbey of Monte Cassino, where his family surely hoped he would one day become abbot. As a teenager he studied at the new University of Naples, where he first met the works of Aristotle.

In 1244 he shocked his family by joining the **Dominicans**, a new order of preaching friars who lived by begging and devoted themselves to study. His family was so opposed that his brothers seized him on the road and held him at home for about a year. Early biographers tell a story that they even sent a woman to tempt him and that he drove her out with a burning stick from the fire; it may be a pious legend. Eventually his family relented.

Thomas went to study with **Albert the Great**, a Dominican with encyclopedic interests in science and Aristotle, first in Paris and then in Cologne. Thomas was big, quiet and slow to speak, and fellow students nicknamed him 'the dumb ox'. According to an early account, Albert replied that one day this ox's bellowing would be heard throughout the world. Again, the story may be embellished, but the prediction came true.

Aquinas became a master of theology at the University of Paris in 1256 and spent the rest of his life teaching in Paris and Italy and writing at an astonishing pace. He wrote commentaries on Aristotle, the *Summa contra Gentiles* (a defense of Christian belief aimed at readers who did not accept scripture), and his masterpiece, the *Summa Theologiae*, a vast textbook of theology begun around 1265. He often dictated to several secretaries at once.

Then, in December 1273, something happened during Mass. He stopped writing. His companion Reginald urged him to continue, and according to the testimony gathered later, Thomas replied that everything he had written seemed like straw compared with what he had seen. The *Summa Theologiae* was never finished. He died in March 1274 at the monastery of Fossanova, aged about forty-nine, on his way to a church council. He was declared a saint in 1323, and in 1879 Pope Leo XIII urged that his philosophy be central to Catholic education.

sections.heading: The Return of Aristotle
sections.body:
To appreciate what Aquinas attempted, recall what the Latin West had to work with. For centuries, as we saw on Day 31, its knowledge of Aristotle was largely limited to the logical works Boethius had translated. Augustine, the great authority, was a Platonist at heart.

That changed in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. In Spain and Sicily, where Christians, Muslims and Jews lived side by side, translators worked through the Arabic library. In Toledo, scholars such as Gerard of Cremona translated dozens of works from Arabic. Others went back to Greek manuscripts; Aquinas' fellow Dominican William of Moerbeke made careful translations directly from the Greek. Within a century, almost all of Aristotle was available in Latin, along with Avicenna's and Averroes' interpretations.

The effect was electric. Aristotle offered a complete, systematic account of nature, the mind, ethics and politics, built on observation and argument rather than authority. But some of his conclusions seemed to clash with Christian teaching. Authorities at Paris banned the public teaching of his works on natural philosophy in 1210 and again in 1215. The bans were soon ignored, and by 1255 Aristotle was required reading. But tensions remained, and in 1270 and 1277 the bishop of Paris condemned lists of philosophical propositions, the second list including a few associated with Aquinas himself.

Aquinas worked in the middle of this storm. On one side were traditionalists who thought Aristotle dangerous. On the other were the **Latin Averroists** (Day 33), who seemed willing to follow Aristotle wherever he led. Aquinas took a third path: accept Aristotle's genuine insights, correct his errors with better arguments, and show that the result fits with faith.

sections.heading: Faith and Reason as Partners
sections.body:
Aquinas' view of faith and reason can be summed up in a phrase from the opening question of the *Summa Theologiae*: **grace does not destroy nature but perfects it**. Reason is a natural gift; revelation does not cancel it but completes it.

He distinguished two kinds of truth about God:

- **Preambles of faith**: truths that human reason can, in principle, prove on its own, such as that God exists and that God is one. These are taught by revelation too, Aquinas says, because few people have the time, ability or training to work them out, and even philosophers make mistakes.
- **Articles of faith**: truths that exceed reason's power and can be known only through revelation, such as the Trinity or the Incarnation. Reason cannot prove them, but it can show that the objections to them are not decisive.

Since both reason and revelation come from God, who is truth itself, they cannot genuinely contradict each other. You will recognize Averroes' principle that truth cannot contradict truth (Day 33), though Aquinas used it to defend Christian doctrine rather than to put demonstration above scripture.

A good test case is the eternity of the world. Aristotle said it was eternal; scripture says it had a beginning. Aquinas, like Maimonides (Day 33), concluded that neither side can be proved by reason. That the world began is known by faith. But he insisted that an eternal created world is not logically impossible: even if the world had always existed, it would still depend on God for its existence at every moment. Keep that point in mind; it is the key to the Five Ways.

Notice also what Aquinas rejected. In the question just before the Five Ways, he considers Anselm's ontological argument (Day 34) and denies that God's existence is self-evident to us. If we knew God's essence completely, we would see that God must exist. But we don't, so we must reason the other way: from effects we can observe to their hidden cause.

sections.heading: The First Three Ways
sections.body:
The Five Ways appear in the *Summa Theologiae*, Part I, question 2, article 3. Aquinas uses the scholastic method from Day 34: he first lists objections to God's existence (including the problem of evil and the claim that nature can explain everything by itself), then gives his answer, then replies to the objections. His answer offers five routes, each starting from a feature of the world we can observe.

**1. The argument from motion.** We see that things change, or in Aristotle's language, are 'moved'. To change is to go from **potentiality** to **actuality**: wood that is potentially hot becomes actually hot. But a thing cannot bring itself from potentiality to actuality; something already actual must do it, as fire makes wood hot. So whatever changes is changed by something else. If that changer is itself being changed, it too needs a changer, and so on. But this cannot go on to infinity, for then there would be no first changer and so no others either, just as a stick moves only because a hand moves it. So there must be a first **unmoved mover**. Aristotle had argued for an unmoved mover too (Day 18).

**2. The argument from efficient causation.** In the world we find an order of **efficient causes**, the things that make other things happen. Nothing causes itself, since it would have to exist before itself. And the chain of causes cannot go back to infinity, or there would be no first cause and therefore no intermediate causes and no final effect. So there is a **first cause**.

**3. The argument from possibility and necessity.** Many things are **contingent**: they come into existence and pass away, so they are able to exist or not exist. If everything were like that, Aquinas reasons, then at some time nothing would have existed, and then nothing could ever have come into existence, so there would be nothing now, which is false. So not everything is contingent; something exists **necessarily**. Some necessary things might get their necessity from something else, but this cannot go on forever. So there must be a being necessary in itself, which causes the necessity of others. This is clearly a cousin of Avicenna's proof (Day 32).

Each of the Ways ends with the same short sentence: and this everyone understands to be God.

sections.heading: The Fourth and Fifth Ways
sections.body:
**4. The argument from gradation.** We find things that are more or less good, more or less true, more or less noble. But 'more' and 'less' are said of things according to how closely they approach a maximum, as something is hotter the closer it comes to what is hottest. So there is something that is truest, best and noblest, and therefore most fully in being. And the maximum in any kind is the cause of everything in that kind. So there is something that causes the being, goodness and every other perfection of all things. This way has the strongest Platonic flavor (think of the Form of the Good on Day 12) and is the one modern readers usually find hardest to accept, since we no longer think, as medieval physics did, that the hottest thing causes the heat in all hot things.

**5. The argument from governance.** We see that things that lack intelligence, like plants, the heavenly bodies or the parts of animals, act for an end. They act always or nearly always in the same way to achieve what is best, which shows that they do so not by chance but by design. But a thing without knowledge cannot aim at a goal unless it is directed by something with knowledge, as an arrow is aimed by an archer. So there is an intelligent being by whom all natural things are directed to their ends. This draws on Aristotle's idea of the **final cause** (Day 18): an acorn 'aims' at becoming an oak.

The fifth way is related to what later became known as the **design argument**, most famously in William Paley's 1802 image of a watch found on a heath. But notice the difference. Paley pointed to intricate, machine-like complexity. Aquinas points to something simpler: the mere fact that natural things act in regular, goal-directed ways at all.

sections.heading: Weighing the Five Ways
sections.body:
The Five Ways have been criticized from every direction. Here are the most important objections, with possible replies.

**Why not an infinite regress?** Couldn't the chain of causes go back forever? Here a common misunderstanding needs clearing up. Aquinas did not think philosophy could prove that the universe had a beginning; we just saw him accept that an eternal world is possible. Elsewhere he even allows that an infinite series of fathers begetting sons is not impossible. His chains are of a different kind, now often called **essentially ordered** series, in which each member acts only because the one above it is acting *right now*. The stone is moved by the stick, which is moved by the hand, which is moved by the person, all at once. In such a series, if no member has causal power of its own, nothing happens at all. Philosophers still debate whether this distinction is as solid as Aquinas thought.

**A logical slip in the Third Way.** From 'each contingent thing at some time does not exist' Aquinas seems to infer 'at some time, nothing existed'. That is like moving from 'every person has a mother' to 'there is one mother of every person'. Many critics see a fallacy here; some defenders argue that Aquinas was relying on extra assumptions or that the argument can be repaired.

**Is the first cause God?** Suppose there is a first mover or a necessary being. Why think it is all-good, all-knowing and the God of Christianity? The sentence 'and this everyone understands to be God' can look like a leap. But the Five Ways are only the beginning: in the questions that follow, Aquinas argues at length that the first cause must be simple, perfect, good, infinite, unchanging and one.

**Has science made them obsolete?** Newton's physics says a body in motion stays in motion without a mover, and Darwin explained how organisms can look designed without a designer. Defenders reply that Aquinas' 'motion' means any change from potential to actual, not just movement in space, and that the fifth way concerns the regularity of natural laws themselves, which evolution presupposes rather than explains. Whether those replies succeed is one of the live debates in philosophy of religion.

Whatever their success, the Five Ways show Aquinas' method: start from the world everyone can see, reason carefully, and follow the argument. Tomorrow (Day 36) we see how the same method shaped his ethics, and how William of Ockham began to unravel the synthesis.

keyQuote.text: Grace does not destroy nature, but perfects it.
keyQuote.source: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q. 1, a. 8, reply to objection 2

modernConnection.title: The Big Bang, a Priest-Physicist and the Question of Nothing
modernConnection.body:
In 1927 the Belgian physicist Georges Lemaître, who was also a Catholic priest, proposed that the universe is expanding, and in 1931 he suggested that it began from a 'primeval atom'. This became the core of the Big Bang theory. In 1951 Pope Pius XII told the Pontifical Academy of Sciences that modern science seemed to bear witness to the moment of creation. Lemaître was uneasy. He thought science and theology should not be mixed this way, and he reportedly persuaded the Pope not to repeat the claim.

Aquinas would have sided with Lemaître. Remember that he did not think reason could prove the world had a beginning; his arguments work even for an eternal universe. Modern cosmological arguments in his tradition therefore focus less on 'what happened first' and more on the question of dependence, or the famous question Leibniz asked (Day 46): why is there something rather than nothing?

That question has resurfaced in popular science. In 2012 the physicist Lawrence Krauss published *A Universe from Nothing*, arguing that quantum physics can explain how a universe could arise from nothing. The philosopher of physics David Albert replied in a sharp review that Krauss's 'nothing' was actually a quantum vacuum governed by physical laws, which is not nothing at all; the question of why those laws and fields exist remains. That is exactly the kind of point Aquinas' Third Way presses.

The fifth way has a modern heir too: the **fine-tuning argument**, which notes that physical constants seem set within narrow ranges that permit life. Critics answer with the possibility of many universes or with the observation that we could only find ourselves in a life-permitting one.

The parallels have limits. Aquinas' physics, with its heavenly spheres and natural places, is gone, and some of his premises depend on it. But the deepest question he asked, whether a world of dependent things can explain itself, is not a question physics alone can settle.

vocabulary.definition: Truths about God, such as that God exists and is one, that Aquinas held can be demonstrated by natural reason as well as known by revelation.
vocabulary.example: For Aquinas, God's existence is a preamble of faith, but the Trinity is not.

vocabulary.definition: Aristotle's distinction between what a thing is capable of becoming (potentiality) and what it currently is (actuality), central to the First Way.
vocabulary.example: Cold water is potentially hot; heated on a stove, it becomes actually hot.

vocabulary.definition: A first source of change that brings others from potentiality to actuality without itself being changed.
vocabulary.example: The First Way argues that a series of things being changed must depend on an unmoved mover.

vocabulary.definition: The agent or thing that brings something about, one of Aristotle's four causes.
vocabulary.example: The sculptor is the efficient cause of the statue.

vocabulary.definition: A chain of causes in which each member acts only because a prior member is acting on it at the same time, as opposed to a chain stretched out through time.
vocabulary.example: A hand moving a stick that moves a stone is an essentially ordered series; a line of grandparents is not.

vocabulary.definition: The end or goal for which something acts or exists; teleology is explanation in terms of such goals.
vocabulary.example: The Fifth Way argues that unintelligent things acting for ends must be directed by an intelligence.

vocabulary.definition: A family of arguments that reason from the existence of change, causes or contingent things to a first cause or necessary being.
vocabulary.example: The first three of the Five Ways are versions of the cosmological argument.

vocabulary.definition: An argument that the order or purposiveness found in nature points to an intelligent designer.
vocabulary.example: Paley's watch on the heath is a famous design argument, related to Aquinas' Fifth Way.

thinkingExercise.title: Trace the Chain
thinkingExercise.prompt: Put the Five Ways to work on ordinary objects, and test whether their key assumptions hold.
steps: Choose something happening right now around you, such as a lamp shining or a plant growing. List what is causing it at this very moment, then what is causing that, and so on, as far as you can go. Is this an essentially ordered series?
Ask yourself honestly: could this chain go on forever with no first member? Write down your instinct and a reason for it.
Pick the one of the Five Ways that seems strongest to you and the one that seems weakest. Write each as numbered premises and a conclusion, and mark the premise you find most doubtful.
Imagine Aquinas replying to your doubt. What would he say? Use what you learned about essentially ordered series or about 'motion' meaning any change.
Finish with a paragraph: if one of the Ways succeeded, how much would it show? A first cause? A necessary being? The God of a particular religion?

summary: Thomas Aquinas (c. 1225–1274), a Dominican friar trained by Albert the Great, became the greatest synthesizer of Aristotle and Christian theology, in the Summa Theologiae and many other works.
The recovery of Aristotle through translations from Arabic and Greek excited and alarmed thirteenth-century Paris; Aquinas steered between traditionalists and Latin Averroists.

For Aquinas, grace perfects nature: reason can prove preambles of faith such as God's existence, while articles of faith like the Trinity are known only by revelation, and the two cannot truly conflict.
The Five Ways argue from motion, efficient causation, contingency, degrees of perfection and the goal-directedness of nature to a first cause 'which everyone understands to be God'.

Critics question the ban on infinite regress, an apparent fallacy in the Third Way, the leap to God and the impact of modern science; defenders stress essentially ordered series and Aquinas' broad sense of change.

quiz.question: Why did Aquinas reject Anselm's ontological argument?
options: Because he thought God does not exist
Because we do not know God's essence well enough, so we must reason from effects to their cause
Because it contradicts scripture
Because Aristotle had already refuted it
quiz.explanation: Aquinas held that God's existence is self-evident in itself but not to us, so it must be shown a posteriori, from observed effects.

quiz.question: Which of these is an article of faith, according to Aquinas, rather than a preamble of faith?
options: God exists
God is one
There is a first cause of change
God is a Trinity of three persons
quiz.explanation: The Trinity exceeds reason's power and is known only by revelation; the others Aquinas thought reason could demonstrate.

quiz.question: What did Aquinas conclude about whether the world had a beginning?
options: Reason proves the world had a beginning
Reason proves the world is eternal
Reason cannot settle the question; that the world began is known by faith
The question is meaningless
quiz.explanation: Like Maimonides, Aquinas thought neither side could be demonstrated, so his proofs of God do not rely on a temporal beginning.

quiz.question: The First Way relies most directly on which Aristotelian idea?
options: The movement from potentiality to actuality
The golden mean
The tripartite soul
The theory of Forms
quiz.explanation: Change is the actualization of a potential, which requires something already actual.

quiz.question: Which example best illustrates an essentially ordered series?
options: A grandmother, mother and daughter
A sequence of kings, each succeeding the last
A row of dominoes that fell yesterday
A hand pushing a stick that is pushing a stone, right now
quiz.explanation: In an essentially ordered series each member acts only because the one before it is acting at the same time.

quiz.question: What is the main criticism of the Third Way's step 'if everything could fail to exist, at some time nothing existed'?
options: It confuses each thing failing to exist at some time with all things failing to exist at the same time
It relies on scripture
It assumes the world is eternal
It contradicts the First Way
quiz.explanation: Critics compare it to inferring 'one mother of everyone' from 'everyone has a mother'.

quiz.question: The Fifth Way argues from which feature of the world?
options: The existence of evil
The degrees of goodness in things
Unintelligent natural things regularly acting toward ends
The fact that we have an idea of God
quiz.explanation: Like an arrow aimed by an archer, goal-directed behavior in things without minds suggests direction by an intelligence.

quiz.question: Aquinas' Five Ways depend on proving that the universe had a beginning in time.
quiz.explanation: Aquinas thought a beginning could not be demonstrated; the Ways concern present dependence, which would hold even for an eternal world.

quiz.question: The University of Paris at one point banned the public teaching of Aristotle's works on natural philosophy.
quiz.explanation: Bans were issued in 1210 and 1215, though by 1255 Aristotle was part of the required curriculum.

quiz.question: Aquinas finished the Summa Theologiae shortly before his death.
quiz.explanation: He stopped writing after an experience in December 1273, reportedly saying his writings seemed like straw, and the Summa was left unfinished.

goDeeper.body:
Modern philosophers have reformulated Aquinas' cosmological reasoning in several ways. One family focuses on the **principle of sufficient reason**, the claim that everything that exists has an explanation. Leibniz (Day 46) argued that even an infinite series of contingent things needs an explanation outside itself. Critics such as Hume (Day 49) replied that once you have explained each member of a series, there is nothing left over to explain about the whole; defenders reply that this misses the question of why there is any series at all. Alexander Pruss has written a book-length defense of the principle; others, such as Graham Oppy, argue that a naturalist can accept a necessary or brute foundation without calling it God.

A second family, revived by Edward Feser and others in the Aristotelian-Thomist tradition, insists that the Five Ways must be read with Aristotle's metaphysics of act and potency, not as early modern 'first event' arguments. On this reading the First Way is about what keeps any change going at this instant, and the first mover is 'pure act', something with no unrealized potential at all. Whether that metaphysics survives modern physics is the real question.

The 'Kalam' cosmological argument, defended by William Lane Craig, takes the opposite route: it argues that the universe began to exist, drawing on al-Kindi and al-Ghazali (Days 32–33) and on Big Bang cosmology. Aquinas would have regarded this premise as unprovable by reason alone, which makes the Kalam a useful contrast. Anthony Kenny's *The Five Ways* (1969) remains the most influential critical analysis, arguing that each Way depends on outdated physics or an invalid inference.

questions: Is an infinite chain of causes with no first member really impossible, or just hard to imagine?
If a cosmological argument proved that a necessary being exists, would that be enough to justify religious belief? What else would be needed?
Aquinas says faith and reason cannot truly conflict. Can you think of a case where they seem to? How would he handle it?
